_about: The herb book. DRAFT: every entry marked "draft": true is waiting to be read before it goes in a release. Cautions and research lines are from US government pages, which are public domain: NCCIH Herbs at a Glance, and from the NIH's LiverTox (NIDDK) and LactMed (NICHD) and the FDA where NCCIH has no page; the wording here is our own plain-English rendering of them. Where those are silent, traditional uses and preparation draw on Wikipedia (and so do two look-alike warnings, for yarrow and burdock), whose text is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/); each such entry credits the article and revision it used, in a source marked with its license. For the pregnancy and nursing safety of hibiscus, raspberry leaf and yarrow, open-access journal articles licensed CC BY are used, each credited with its license in that herb's sources. Preparation amounts, times and tastes are ordinary kitchen practice and are not tied to a source. Each use carries the Finder's needs (sleep, calm, digestion, colds, sore-throat, nausea, headache, period-cramps, pregnancy, nursing). tools/check-cautions.py checks this file. Every text line names, in "src" (or a field's "...Src"), the ids of the entry's sources it came from, or a shared source in "sharedSources" (kitchen practice; this book's own wording); every source names its license (public-domain, cc-by-3.0, cc-by-4.0, cc-by-sa-4.0, own, none; own is text by the app's author, wander wildwood, usable in this app and in his game). tools/game-safe.py lists which lines may go into a CC BY-NC-ND work.

herbs.name: Chamomile
herbs.taste: Mild and sweet, a little like apples

cautions.text: Allergy: it can cause allergic reactions, rarely severe ones (anaphylaxis). These are more likely if you are allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds or daisies.
It may act a little like estrogen. It might make birth control pills work less well, and might worsen a condition sensitive to estrogen, such as breast or uterine cancer.

Interactions have been reported with warfarin (a blood thinner) and with some drugs the liver breaks down, and it might add to sedatives. If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. A 2021 review links drinking a lot of chamomile tea in pregnancy to early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Side effects are uncommon: nausea and dizziness. Near the eyes it can irritate them.

interactions: drugs broken down by the liver
herbs.research: Not enough reliable evidence to say; some early studies suggest it may help anxiety, and the one study on sleeplessness found no benefit.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried flowers per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: NCCIH, Chamomile (Herbs at a Glance)
Phytotherapy in obstetrics: therapeutic indications, limits, and dangers (Journal of Medicine and Life, 2021)
sources.authors: Grigoriu C, Varlas V, Călinescu G, et al.

herbs.name: Comfrey
herbs.dontUseReason: Comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Taken by mouth it can block the small veins of the liver (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) and cause severe liver injury.

cautions.text: Don't take comfrey by mouth, as a tea or in any other form.
Babies and children seem especially sensitive to its poison. Pregnancy, nursing and children: don't use it. Ask your midwife or doctor about anything you have already taken.

uses.evidence: not a reason to take it

uses.for: pain and swelling from arthritis, sprains and broken bones
uses.evidence: not a reason to take it

herbs.research: Whatever it was used for, it is not safe to take by mouth.

sources.title: LiverTox (NIDDK), Comfrey
PubMed record of the LiverTox entry

herbs.name: Ginger
herbs.parts: Rhizome (the underground stem, called the root)

cautions.text: If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy: it may be safe and has been studied for morning sickness, but ask your midwife or doctor first. Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe.
Side effects can include stomach discomfort, heartburn, diarrhea, and mouth and throat irritation.

uses.evidence: some evidence, for ginger supplements in pregnancy

herbs.research: Research, mostly on supplements rather than tea, suggests it may help nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and may ease period cramps; most studies found it no help for motion sickness.

preparation.amount: About an inch of fresh root, sliced thin, per cup
preparation.note: Simmer it gently in a covered pan, then strain.

sources.title: NCCIH, Ginger (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Peppermint
herbs.parts: Leaves; the oil comes from the leaves and flowering tops

cautions.text: Children: never put peppermint oil on the face of a baby or young child, or let them breathe it in. The menthol in it can cause serious breathing problems.
Peppermint oil taken by mouth can cause heartburn, nausea, stomach pain and a dry mouth, and on its own it may make indigestion worse for some people.
Pregnancy and nursing: peppermint in food amounts is likely safe; little is known about larger, medicinal amounts. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before using any herbal product.
On the skin the oil can cause rashes and irritation. Rarely, it causes allergic reactions.
Peppermint tea appears to be safe, but the long-term safety of large amounts of the leaf is unknown.

uses.evidence: not enough evidence for the leaf
some evidence, for the oil in coated capsules
a small amount of evidence, for the oil during chemotherapy
a little evidence, for the oil on the skin

herbs.research: Very little research on the leaf tea; some evidence that peppermint oil in coated capsules eases IBS.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Peppermint Oil (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: St John's wort

cautions.text: It interacts in dangerous, sometimes life-threatening ways with many medicines. If you take any medicine at all, don't use it without asking your doctor or pharmacist.

It can weaken: some antidepressants (amitriptyline, bupropion); birth control pills; cyclosporine, which keeps a transplanted organ from being rejected; some seizure medicines (phenytoin, carbamazepine); some heart medicines (digoxin, ivabradine); some HIV drugs (indinavir, nevirapine); some cancer medicines (irinotecan, imatinib, docetaxel); warfarin, a blood thinner; and some statins (simvastatin).
Taken with some antidepressants or other drugs that affect serotonin, it can cause serious serotonin-related side effects.
Pregnancy: it may be unsafe, as it may increase the risk of birth defects. Nursing: babies of mothers who take it can have colic, drowsiness and lethargy. Ask your midwife or doctor.
In large doses, or on the skin, it may cause severe skin reactions in sunlight.
Depression can be a serious illness. If you or someone in your family may have depression, see a doctor.
Other side effects can include diarrhea, dizziness, trouble sleeping, restlessness and tingling skin.

uses.evidence: evidence it may help mild or moderate depression for up to 12 weeks

herbs.research: It may help mild or moderate depression, but it interacts with many medicines; for other uses there is not enough evidence.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried flowering tops per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, St. John's Wort (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Spearmint
herbs.taste: Sweet and cool, milder than peppermint

cautions.text: There is no NIH summary of this herb's safety, so little is known about it beyond its use in food and tea.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy and nursing: not enough is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it, and this book found no US government summary of the research, so it makes no claim about whether it helps.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves, or a small handful of fresh, per cup

sources.title: Wikipedia, Spearmint (traditional use and preparation only)

herbs.name: Lemon balm

cautions.text: If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy: not enough is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Nursing: it has not been studied on its own, but in usual amounts it is not likely to harm a nursing baby. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
It is usually well tolerated. Now and then people have had nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, dizziness or wheezing.

uses.evidence: weak evidence, in mixtures with other herbs

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it. LiverTox finds no liver harm from it; LactMed finds weak evidence that it helps milk supply.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: LiverTox (NIDDK), Lemon Balm
LactMed (NICHD), Lemon Balm

herbs.name: Lavender

cautions.text: It might add to the effect of sedatives (medicines or herbs that make you sleepy). This matters most before an operation. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Children: a few cases of breast swelling have been reported in children who used products with lavender on the skin. It is not clear the lavender caused it.
Pregnancy: little is known about whether it is safe. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that can stimulate the womb, which may risk miscarriage or early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Depression can be a serious illness. If you or someone in your family may have depression, see a doctor.
By mouth it can cause diarrhea, headache, nausea or burping. On the skin it can cause allergic rashes. As aromatherapy it can cause headache or coughing.

uses.evidence: some evidence, for a lavender oil product taken by mouth

herbs.research: More good research is needed to say whether it helps. Studies suggest a lavender oil product taken by mouth might help anxiety; for sleep, it is unclear.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried flowers per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: NCCIH, Lavender (Herbs at a Glance)
Phytotherapy in obstetrics: therapeutic indications, limits, and dangers (Journal of Medicine and Life, 2021)

herbs.name: Valerian
herbs.taste: Earthy and bitter, with a strong smell

cautions.text: Don't take it with alcohol or sedatives (medicines that make you sleepy).
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.

It seems safe for most adults for a few weeks; the safety of long use is unknown. Stopping suddenly after long use can bring anxiety, irritability, heart disturbances, trouble sleeping and, rarely, hallucinations.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Side effects can include headache, upset stomach, dullness, restlessness and vivid dreams. Very rarely, liver injury has been reported, mostly with other herbs.

herbs.research: There is not enough evidence to say whether it helps any condition. The evidence on sleep is inconsistent, and a sleep medicine society advises against it for long-term insomnia in adults.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of dried root per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: NCCIH, Valerian (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Passionflower

cautions.text: Pregnancy: don't use it. It may bring on contractions of the womb. Ask your midwife or doctor.

Before an operation: don't take it unless your doctor says so. With anesthesia and other medicines given around surgery it might slow the nervous system too much. Tell your doctor if you have taken it in the 2 weeks before.
Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
As a tea it may be safe for up to a week of nights. It can cause drowsiness, dizziness and confusion.

interactions: anesthesia and medicines given around surgery

uses.evidence: a small amount of research, with mixed results

herbs.research: A small amount of research suggests it might ease anxiety and lengthen sleep, but the results are not definite.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of dried herb per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Passionflower (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Echinacea
herbs.taste: Earthy; it makes the tongue tingle

cautions.text: Allergy: some people have allergic reactions to it, which may be severe. It is related to ragweed, daisies and sunflowers.
Children: some children in a study got rashes, perhaps from allergy. Ask the child's doctor before giving it.
It might interact with medicines that calm the immune system, with caffeine, and with some drugs the liver breaks down. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Pregnancy: extracts may be safe for up to 7 days early in pregnancy, but ask your midwife or doctor first. Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe.
The most common side effects are stomach pain and nausea.

interactions: medicines that calm the immune system
drugs broken down by the liver

uses.evidence: it may slightly lower your chance of catching one

herbs.research: Taking echinacea may slightly reduce your chances of catching a cold; it is still unclear whether it can shorten one.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried root or herb per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: NCCIH, Echinacea (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Elderberry
herbs.taste: Fruity and dark, a little tart

cautions.text: Don't eat raw or unripe berries, or the leaves, stems or bark. They contain a poison that releases cyanide and can cause nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhea. Cooking the ripe berries removes it.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether it is safe for health purposes. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Rarely, it causes allergic reactions.

herbs.research: Some early research suggests it may ease the symptoms of flu, colds and other upper respiratory infections. There is no good evidence that it helps COVID-19.

preparation.amount: 1 tablespoon of dried ripe berries per cup
preparation.note: Simmer the berries gently, then strain. Never use raw berries.

sources.title: NCCIH, Elderberry (Herbs at a Glance)
LactMed (NICHD), Elderberry

If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy and nursing: not enough is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.

herbs.research: NCCIH covers the berry, not the flower, and this book found no US government summary of research on the flower, so it makes no claim about whether it helps.

preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

herbs.taste: Savory, warm and a little bitter

cautions.text: Pregnancy: it may be unsafe, because a substance in it (thujone) may be harmful. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that can stimulate the womb, which may risk miscarriage or early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor.
Sage contains thujone, which can be toxic in large amounts. It may be unsafe in high doses or taken for a long time. Food amounts are likely safe.
Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that may lower milk supply. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.

herbs.research: Only small amounts of research exist. A few small studies suggest it might reduce hot flashes and may help memory and cholesterol.

herbs.taste: Mild and sweet; it makes a slippery tea

Nursing: it has not been studied, but it is unlikely to harm a nursing baby. Ask your midwife or doctor first.

herbs.name: Licorice root

cautions.text: Don't take it if you have high blood pressure, a heart or kidney condition, or eat a lot of salt. Even small amounts have caused severe harm in these people.

Pregnancy: large amounts are unsafe and can bring on early birth. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that can stimulate the womb, which may risk miscarriage or early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor. Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe.
A substance in it (glycyrrhizin) can cause serious harm, such as an irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest, especially in large amounts or over a long time.
Interactions with corticosteroids (steroid medicines) have been reported. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Licorice without glycyrrhizin (DGL) might be safe for up to 4 months. On the skin it can cause irritation.

uses.evidence: some evidence, for a gargle or lozenge after surgery
some evidence, for a mouth rinse

herbs.research: There isn't enough good evidence to support it for any condition. A licorice gargle or rinse might help canker sores and a sore throat after surgery.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of dried root per cup
preparation.note: Not for every day over a long time.

sources.title: NCCIH, Licorice Root (Herbs at a Glance)
Phytotherapy in obstetrics: therapeutic indications, limits, and dangers (Journal of Medicine and Life, 2021)
sources.authors: Grigoriu C, Varlas V, Călinescu G, et al.

herbs.name: Fennel

cautions.text: Allergy: don't use it if you, or your baby, are allergic to carrots, celery or other plants of the carrot family.
It can make the skin more sensitive to sunlight. Avoid strong sun while you use it.

Nursing: in usual amounts it is not likely to harm a nursing baby, and some sources say to use it for no more than 2 weeks. Too much of an herbal tea with fennel and anise made two newborns ill. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Pregnancy: not enough is known about whether it is safe. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that can stimulate the womb, which may risk miscarriage or early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Raised liver tests have been reported in a woman taking a milk-supply tea that contains fennel.

uses.evidence: two small studies found some increase

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it. LactMed: two small studies found some increase in milk with fennel, but no rise in the milk hormone.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of seeds, lightly crushed, per cup
preparation.note: Cover the cup while it steeps.

sources.title: LactMed (NICHD), Fennel
Phytotherapy in obstetrics: therapeutic indications, limits, and dangers (Journal of Medicine and Life, 2021)

herbs.name: Dandelion
herbs.taste: Bitter; the roasted root tastes a little like coffee

cautions.text: It might interact with diabetes medicines, blood thinners and water pills (diuretics), among others. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Allergy: on the skin it may cause a reaction in people with eczema. It is not clear whether people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds or daisies react to it.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether more than food amounts are safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Food amounts are likely safe; less is known about larger amounts.

herbs.research: There is no compelling evidence that it helps any condition; very little research exists.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried root per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Dandelion (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Nettle
herbs.parts: Leaves (dried or cooked; the root is used apart)

cautions.text: Fresh leaves sting; don't eat or drink them raw. Drying or cooking takes the sting away.
Nursing: don't put nettle on the breast; one nursing baby got a rash. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that may lower milk supply. Ask your midwife or doctor before using it while nursing.
Pregnancy: not enough is known about whether it is safe. A 2021 review lists it among herbs that can stimulate the womb, which may risk miscarriage or early birth. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
It is generally well tolerated, and has not been linked to liver harm.
Rarely, weeks of nettle tea have been linked to hormone effects such as breast swelling or milk leaking; these went away after stopping.

uses.for: urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate (the root)

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it. LiverTox: the claims for the leaf have not been shown in good studies; the root has been reported to ease urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves per cup

sources.title: LiverTox (NIDDK), Stinging Nettle
LactMed (NICHD), Stinging Nettle

herbs.name: Hibiscus
herbs.parts: Calyces (the red cups around the flower)

cautions.text: Pregnancy: it has not been studied in pregnant people. In pregnant rats, large doses of an extract harmed the newborns' cells, and the researchers advise using it only with a health professional's guidance. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Nursing: nothing is known about whether it reaches breast milk or is safe for a nursing baby. Ask your midwife or doctor first.

It can lower blood pressure, and it might interact with blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors such as ramipril); this has not been studied. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
The NIH's only summary of it (LactMed) is about mothers' milk, so little is known about its safety beyond its use in food and tea.
It is generally well tolerated, but allergic reactions are possible, including in people allergic to marshmallow. Very large doses of extract affected liver tests in one study.

uses.for: flavor and color, as an everyday tea

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it, and this book found no US government summary of the research, so it makes no claim about whether it helps.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried calyces per cup
preparation.note: It is also good steeped and served cold.

cautions.text: There is no NIH summary of this herb's safety, so little is known about it beyond its use in food and tea.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy and nursing: not enough is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.

herbs.name: Turmeric
herbs.taste: Earthy, warm and a little bitter

cautions.text: Pregnancy: turmeric supplements may be unsafe. Food amounts are a different matter; ask your midwife or doctor. Nursing: little is known about more than food amounts.
Liver damage has been reported with curcumin products made to be better absorbed. If you notice tiredness, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine or yellow skin, stop and see your doctor.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
By mouth it can cause nausea, vomiting, reflux, an upset stomach, diarrhea or constipation. On the skin it can cause hives or itching.

uses.evidence: early positive evidence, for knee arthritis

herbs.research: Not enough is known to say whether turmeric or curcumin helps any condition. Early evidence for knee arthritis is positive but needs better studies.

preparation.amount: 1/2 teaspoon of ground turmeric, or a thin slice of fresh root, per cup
preparation.note: Simmer gently, then strain.

sources.title: NCCIH, Turmeric (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Cinnamon

cautions.text: Pregnancy: food amounts seem safe, but larger amounts of Ceylon cinnamon are considered unsafe. Ask your midwife or doctor. Nursing: little is known about larger amounts.
Cassia cinnamon, the common kind in North America, can contain a lot of coumarin, which affects the liver. Long use may be a problem for people with liver disease.
In larger amounts or over a long time it can cause stomach problems or allergic reactions.
It might interact with a cancer medicine and with nicotine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Never swallow a spoonful of the powder (the "cinnamon challenge"). Serious harm is possible.
On the skin the oil or powder can cause irritation.

herbs.research: Research doesn't clearly support using cinnamon for any health condition.

preparation.amount: 1 cinnamon stick, broken, per cup
preparation.note: Simmer gently, then strain.

sources.title: NCCIH, Cinnamon (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Raspberry leaf

cautions.text: Pregnancy: it is traditionally drunk late in pregnancy to prepare for birth, and it may make the womb contract. There is too little research to call it safe: one small study saw no safety problems, but its authors warn that this is not proof of safety. Ask your midwife or doctor before using it.
Nursing: as a tea it is usually without side effects, but there is no information on safety while nursing. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
The NIH's only summary of it (LactMed) is about mothers' milk, so little is known about its safety beyond its use in food and tea.

uses.for: preparing for childbirth, late in pregnancy

herbs.research: NCCIH has no page on it. LactMed finds no good studies on milk supply. For birth, one small study saw fewer labors needing to be sped up, but it cannot be relied on; a proper trial is needed.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves per cup

herbs.name: Hawthorn

cautions.text: Don't take supplements labeled "tejocote root" (Mexican hawthorn). The FDA found some contain yellow oleander, a toxic plant, and warned they can cause severe harm or death.

Heart medicines: in one study a hawthorn preparation may have worsened heart failure, perhaps by interacting with the patients' medicines. If you have a heart condition or take any medicine, ask your doctor first.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
It has not been tested for more than 16 weeks. Side effects can include dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and muscle pain.

herbs.research: There is little or no good evidence on hawthorn for most conditions; the evidence on heart failure is conflicting.

preparation.amount: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaves and flowers per cup

herbs.name: Milk thistle
herbs.taste: Mild, oily and a little bitter

cautions.text: Allergy: it may cause allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds or daisies.
Supplements vary: some held much more or less silymarin than the label said, or were contaminated with pesticides, germs or mold poisons.
If you take any medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
Pregnancy and nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
It is usually well tolerated. The most common side effects are bloating, nausea and gas.

herbs.research: There isn't enough good evidence to reach firm conclusions; trials for liver diseases have been conflicting or too limited.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of seeds, crushed, per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Milk Thistle (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Feverfew

cautions.text: Pregnancy: don't take it. It may affect contractions of the womb. Ask your midwife or doctor.
Before an operation: it may slow blood clotting; stop it at least 2 weeks before.
It may interact with some medicines, including migraine medicines. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Allergy: people sensitive to ragweed and related plants may react to it.
Nursing: little is known about whether it is safe. Ask your midwife or doctor first.
Side effects can include nausea, digestive trouble and bloating. Chewing fresh leaves can cause mouth sores; on the skin it can cause a rash.

uses.evidence: mixed results; some research suggests fewer migraines

herbs.research: Some research suggests it may help prevent migraine headaches, but results have been mixed.

preparation.amount: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon of dried leaves per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Feverfew (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Ginkgo

cautions.text: Don't take it with blood thinners such as warfarin: it may raise the risk of bleeding.
Don't eat the seeds or the crude plant. Fresh seeds are toxic, and roasted seeds have caused serious harm.
Pregnancy: it may be unsafe; near the birth it might bring on early labor or extra bleeding. Ask your midwife or doctor. Nursing: little is known.
It may interact with other medicines too. Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Leaf extract is usually well tolerated; the most common side effects are dizziness, stomach upset and headache.

uses.evidence: a small amount of evidence, not conclusive

herbs.research: There's no conclusive evidence that ginkgo helps any health condition; it did not prevent dementia in large studies.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of dried leaves per cup
preparation.note: Leaves only, never the seeds.

sources.title: NCCIH, Ginkgo (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Ginseng

cautions.text: Pregnancy: it may be unsafe; a substance in it has caused birth defects in animals. Some experts advise against it for infants, children, and anyone pregnant or nursing. Ask your midwife or doctor.
Diabetes: it might lower blood sugar. If you have diabetes, ask your doctor first.
It may worsen autoimmune disorders and interfere with blood clotting. It might interact with some medicines; ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any.
Rarely, it has caused a severe rash, liver damage or severe allergic reactions.
Trouble sleeping is its most common side effect. Up to 6 months seems safe for most people; long-term safety is uncertain.

uses.evidence: a small effect in some studies
a very small amount of early research

herbs.research: Most studies have been small and short. It may have a small effect on general tiredness; the research on other uses is inconclusive.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of sliced dried root per cup

sources.title: NCCIH, Asian Ginseng (Herbs at a Glance)

herbs.name: Green tea
herbs.taste: Fresh and grassy; it turns bitter if steeped too hot or too long

cautions.text: It contains caffeine. For most adults the FDA cites 400 mg of caffeine a day (about two to three 12-ounce cups of coffee) as an amount not generally linked to harm. Too much can cause a racing heart, jitters, trouble sleeping, an upset stomach and headache.

Pregnancy: keep caffeine moderate, and ask your midwife or doctor about it. Nursing: caffeine passes into breast milk; a lot of it can make a baby fussy and sleep poorly. Low to moderate amounts usually cause no trouble.

In large amounts it lowers the effect of nadolol (a beta-blocker for blood pressure and the heart); extracts lower atorvastatin (a cholesterol medicine); and it interacts with raloxifene (a bone medicine). Ask your doctor or pharmacist first if you take any medicine.
Children: caffeinated drinks are best avoided under age 2.
As a drink it has no reported safety concerns for adults. Rarely, liver injury has been reported, mostly with extract tablets and capsules.

uses.evidence: a small reduction, mostly with extracts

herbs.research: Definite conclusions cannot yet be reached for most uses; it lowered cholesterol a little in studies, mostly of extracts.

preparation.amount: 1 teaspoon of leaves per cup
preparation.note: Water well off the boil; hotter water makes it bitter.

sources.title: NCCIH, Green Tea (Herbs at a Glance)
FDA, Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine is Too Much?

herbs.name: Black tea
herbs.taste: Strong, malty and a little astringent

cautions.text: It contains caffeine. For most adults the FDA cites 400 mg of caffeine a day (about two to three 12-ounce cups of coffee) as an amount not generally linked to harm. Too much can cause a racing heart, jitters, trouble sleeping, an upset stomach and headache.
Pregnancy and nursing: ask your midwife or doctor whether you should limit caffeine. Caffeine passes into breast milk; a lot of it can make a baby fussy and sleep poorly.
Children: caffeinated drinks are best avoided under age 2.
Some medicines and conditions make people more sensitive to caffeine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you take any medicine.
Caffeine in usual amounts has not been linked to liver harm.

herbs.name: Pennyroyal
herbs.dontUseReason: Pennyroyal oil is highly toxic. Small amounts have caused seizures, coma, collapse of the heart and lungs, liver and kidney failure, and death.
herbs.parts: Leaves; the oil comes from them

cautions.text: Don't take pennyroyal oil by mouth in any amount. Even a tablespoon has killed people.
Pregnancy: never use it. It has been taken to end pregnancies, and the amounts used can kill. Ask your midwife or doctor about anything you have already taken.
The tea and leaf have been used without serious harm, but they hold the same poison (pulegone) as the oil. This book does not recommend them.

uses.evidence: not a reason to take it
not a reason to take it

herbs.research: Whatever it was used for, the oil is not safe to take by mouth.

sources.title: LiverTox (NIDDK), Pennyroyal Oil

herbs.name: Kava
herbs.dontUseReason: Kava has been linked to liver injury, sometimes serious or fatal, including from drinks made with water. No one can yet say who is at risk.

cautions.text: Don't take kava, as a drink, a supplement or in any other form.
Don't take it with alcohol or with sedatives (such as benzodiazepines).
Pregnancy and nursing: it may carry special risks then. Don't use it. Ask your midwife or doctor about anything you have already taken.
Other side effects include upset stomach, headache and dizziness; long, heavy use can cause dry, scaly, yellowed skin.

uses.evidence: not a reason to take it

herbs.research: Kava supplements may help anxiety, but the risk to the liver outweighs that.

sources.title: NCCIH, Kava (Herbs at a Glance)
LiverTox (NIDDK), Kava Kava

herbs.name: Ephedra
herbs.dontUseReason: Ephedra has been linked to high blood pressure, heart attack, seizure, stroke and psychosis, even at low doses and for a short time. The FDA banned it in dietary supplements.

cautions.text: Don't take ephedra in any form. Supplements containing it are banned in the US.
Pregnancy, nursing and children: it is considered unsafe. Ask your midwife or doctor about anything you have already taken.
It is especially risky for people with heart or blood vessel disease, and with other stimulants such as caffeine.
It can also cause anxiety, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn, sleeplessness, irritability and nausea.

uses.evidence: not a reason to take it
not a reason to take it

herbs.research: Before the ban, research showed a small short-term effect on weight, far outweighed by its risks.

sources.title: NCCIH, Ephedra (Herbs at a Glance)
